scenes.narration: Here is the one name we have. Word is tied to the string Palolem. Indexing and slicing do not change that string. Every slice makes a new string, and prints it, and forgets it, unless we tie a name to it. The original string is untouched. That fits with what we learned in the last episode.

scenes.onScreen: reverse.py: a third number in the slice sets the step

scenes.narration: [HL 1] The same word. [HL 2] A slice can have a third number, the step. A step of minus one walks backwards. So the word prints reversed, m, e, l, o, l, a, P. [HL 3] A step of two takes every second letter, positions zero, two, four, six. P, l, l, m. [HL 4] The length is seven. The last valid index is always the length minus one.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: an index too far
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the Python error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding

shorts.title: Positions start at zero
shorts.hook: "Every character in a string has a position, called an index."
shorts.script: Every character in a string has a position, called an index. The first one is zero, not one. So the word Palolem has indexes zero to six. Pick one with square brackets. Word, bracket zero, gives P. Think of a row of beach huts, numbered from zero. This is the same in almost every programming language, so learn it once. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Counting from zero.

shorts.title: Negative indexes
shorts.script: Negative indexes count from the end. Minus one is the last character. Minus two is the second last. So word, bracket, minus one, gives m, whatever the length of the word. It is the easiest way to grab the last letter, and you never need to count. Use negative indexes whenever you care about the end of a string. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Count from the end.

shorts.title: Slices
shorts.hook: "A slice cuts a piece of a string."
shorts.script: A slice cuts a piece of a string. Word, bracket, one, colon, four, gives positions one, two and three. The start is included, and the stop is not, just like range. Leave out the start, and it begins at the beginning. Leave out the stop, and it runs to the end. One tool, many pieces, and the original is untouched. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Start included, stop not.

shorts.title: Index error
shorts.hook: "Here is the classic out of range bug."
shorts.script: Here is the classic out of range bug. Palolem has seven letters, so the indexes are zero to six. Ask for index seven, and Python says, index error, string index out of range. The last index is always the length minus one. Or just use minus one. When you see this error, count again, starting from zero. Then run it, and compare with what you predicted. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Count from zero.

shorts.title: Pun and challenge
shorts.hook: "Why did the string stay calm in the slicing class?"
shorts.script: Why did the string stay calm in the slicing class? It knew where to cut. Your challenge. Take the word Calangute. Print the first three letters using a slice. Then print the last three letters, using a negative index inside the slice. Remember, you can leave out the start or the stop. Post your two answers in the comments. Keep coding, says Xecxec! Full video: EP 24.
